cells.tense: You are here, with the pen, alive to what a situation is asking for before it says it.
cells.ask: Say one feeling out loud today before you've decided it's fair to say it — even if the wording comes out clumsy.
cells.core:
You're not holding anything off. Something comes up — a room, a person, a mood — and you sense its shape before it's named, and you move. You're curious about what you don't know yet instead of braced against it. That's working right now. The fairness you carry shows up in how you adjust, not in anything you announce. You feel something, you take it in, and where it settles changes the room. You're not running a system; you're reading what's in front of you and staying with it.

So the act for this moment is small: put one of those readings into words before you've checked whether it's fair to say it. Not a speech, not a correction — just the thing you noticed, spoken while it's still live. That's the edge this is asking for, and it's also where the balance keeps itself: not in being right, but in the habit of bringing what you sense into the open where it can be answered.
cells.sheetLine: You sense the situation and move — balance holds by staying in contact.
cells.verb: Sensing what hasn't happened yet and walking into it with beginner's eyes — open to it, not managing it
cells.place: The square where what's out of proportion gets put back, and the fixing is quiet, not a punishment

cells.tense: You are leaning into a version of how this should go that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.ask: Catch the moment you start rehearsing how a conversation will go today. When you notice it, name one thing that's actually happening in the room instead.
cells.core:
You're ahead of the room. Before the conversation happens, you've already run it — how it should go, where it could tip, how to make it fair. And the sensing you're so good at has started working for the rehearsal instead of the moment in front of you. The care underneath is real; you want things to come out even. But the evenness in your head keeps not matching the room, and the gap costs you more than the miss would. The fairness you're reaching for doesn't need a plan; it needs you in the present, reading what's actually here.

So try catching the moment you start playing it forward. When you feel it — the second or two before you go into prep mode — say one true thing about what's in front of you instead. One sentence, out loud or on paper. It doesn't fix anything. It just puts you back where your sense can do its work.

cells.tense: You are still standing at the edge of something you've already passed, holding back the sense you used to trust.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you notice today — a mood, a shift in someone's face — and act on it once without waiting to be sure it's fair to trust.
cells.core:
The sensing is still there. Someone shifts their tone and you catch it; something goes quiet and you know why. But you're not doing anything with it. You wait for the feeling to be confirmed before you let it move you, and by the time confirmation comes, the moment has passed. Fairness sits in front of the feeling now: don't act until you're certain it's deserved, don't speak until you can show the work. So nothing moves. You're not short on intuition; you're short on permission to act before you're sure. The threshold you're standing at is one you've already crossed.

So choose one thing today — a look, a tone, a change in the air — and let it carry you to one small act before you've settled whether it's fair. Not a confrontation. A response.

cells.tense: You are already moving with a reading of the room that you keep describing as just how it is.
cells.ask: Write one sentence tonight about why you moved on a feeling this week — not a justification, just the account, in your own words.
cells.core:
You're doing it right now. Someone says one thing and you've already read the undercurrent and adjusted. That's the sensing working. But when you describe it, it comes out as just noticing, just being practical, just keeping things fair. The reading is real and it's yours, and you keep handing the credit to the situation — as if the room told you what it meant, and you only followed. That works until it doesn't; you start half-answering your own questions, moving on instincts you won't claim, and the fairness gets decided by something you won't put your name on. The instrument is on. The claim to it isn't.

So tonight, pick one move you made this week — one adjustment, one response — and write down what you sensed and why you acted. It's not confession. It's just the account, in your own words, so the power has a place to come back to.

A reader could reasonably say 'it's not about fairness, it's just that nothing feels solid right now,' and the ask still has to be useful: so each ask is a small act they can do whether or not my read of the seat is right. The sentence that serves me more than them is the tidy 'here's what it's like to be in the feedback loop' — so I cut that and kept their words plain.
